title: TickTick Alternatives in 2026, Chosen by Complaint
summary: TickTick alternatives include four task managers ranked by pricing, platform support, sharing, and integration. Decide which fits your workflow best.
body_markdown:
## Activepieces


Activepieces isn't a TickTick replacement; it's open-source workflow automation with an MIT-licensed core, and it answers the complaint that TickTick doesn't connect to the rest of your tools with 750 integrations counted from its monorepo on GitHub, so your tool is probably already there.


When a form response or a Slack message should become a task, an Activepieces flow can create that task in Todoist or Microsoft To Do without you copying anything by hand, and the free plan allows unlimited flows, with a run costing 1 credit however many steps it has.


The flow has three parts. A trigger fires when a form response arrives or a Slack message matches a rule, the flow reshapes the fields, and an action writes a new task into the app you moved to.


Read left to right, the illustration below shows that path. The point to take from it is that you build the connection once and the to-do app never needs to know where the task came from.


### How many connectors exist


Whether your particular pairing exists depends on the catalog of connectors, which[Activepieces](https://www.activepieces.com/blog/activepieces-integrations-list-for-2026-by-category) calls pieces, and it has grown quickly.


[Activepieces](https://www.activepieces.com/pieces) lists 200 integrations in June 2024 and 280 in March 2025, which means the platform had grown its integration catalog by 40 percent within nine months. The first nine months added about 80.


By September 2025 Activepieces had reached 400, and by November 2025 500, which means 100 integrations arrived in two months. The count was 772 in October 2026 and 775 in November 2026.


In that last month growth is much slower, but the larger point stands: a tool missing from the catalog a year ago is now fairly likely to be there.


The count comes from the packages/integrations/community directory of the open-source monorepo on GitHub, where every integration has its own folder and the core is MIT-licensed, and roughly 60% of the integrations in it were contributed by the community rather than the company, so maintenance of most integrations doesn't depend on a single company.


A count of 775 says nothing about whether your two apps are among them, but their folders in that directory do.


### Self-hosting


Because the code is open source, you can also run it on your own server instead of using the hosted version. That's useful if the tasks contain client data you would rather not send through a third party.


The cost is that you maintain the server, apply the updates, and fix the flow when an upstream API changes.


### When task automation isn't the answer


When not to bother: if your frustration is price, platform fit or sharing a list with a team, automation fixes none of them.


A flow that fills a task list only helps if you were already doing that copying by hand, and if you do it twice a month, the setup time will exceed the time you save.
